lines: In 1963, a man fixing up his house knocked through a wall. Behind it was a tunnel, and below his town, a whole city, eighty five meters deep.
Long ago, volcanoes buried this region in thick ash. It hardened into tuff, a rock soft enough to carve with hand tools. So instead of building up, people dug down.
Step one: carve, don't build. Start from a shaft, then cut rooms out of the rock, one level below the next.
Step two: air. More than fifty shafts bring fresh air down from the surface. The deepest, about fifty five meters, was also used as a well.
Step three: everything a town needs. Stables, kitchens, wine and oil presses, storerooms, and even a church.
Now the clever part: round stone doors, up to half a tonne each. They only move from the inside, so every level can be sealed off on its own.
Archaeologists think the city goes down as many as eighteen levels. Only eight are open to visitors today.
At its peak, it could shelter about twenty thousand people, with their animals and food. All of it, carved by hand.
